answer: In the LINE paper (Tang et al., 2015, "LINE: Large-scale Information Network Embedding"), second-order proximity is applicable to directed and undirected networks (it is specifically designed for directed graphs, where a vertex's role as a context/neighbor differs from its role as a node, though it applies to undirected graphs as well). It captures the proximity between a pair of vertices through their shared neighborhoods: two vertices are considered similar if they share many common neighbors, i.e., vertices with similar neighborhood structures (neighbor distributions) are assumed to be similar, even if they are not directly linked. Second-order proximity is thus used when first-order proximity (direct ties) is sparse or absent, and it is modeled by giving each vertex a separate 'context' embedding for when it acts as a neighbor.
